name: Four Corners Along a Three-Cube Path Preserve the Endpoint
statement: Let an ample family $H$ contain a three-cube and let $c,a,z,v$ be degree-three corners forming a shortest three-edge path between opposite cube vertices. Then $H$ peels to $a$ if and only if $H\setminus\{c\}$ peels to $a$.
proof: Assume a minimum counterexample. Square-pair invariance excludes the two other neighbors of $c$ as corners, and the opposite-edge theorem excludes the remaining opposite corner. Commutation of nonadjacent corner deletions then forces every successful peeling to start with the next two marked path vertices and a uniquely determined third cube vertex. These four vertices form an entire peripheral square restriction. The peripheral endpoint criterion yields a first corner outside that square; it is simultaneously a corner of $H$ and $H-c$, and deleting it produces a smaller counterexample, a contradiction.
